hazards.behind-the-jack: You stepped in behind the ram. A tendon holds its energy along its own axis, so a strand that snaps or a wedge that does not hold comes back out of the anchorage the way the jack is pointing, at a speed nothing stops. That space is the one place on this deck nobody stands in without a reason to be there, and OSHA 1926.701(c) is written that way: no employee behind the jack during tensioning except the ones essential to the operation, with signs and barriers keeping everybody else out of the area. Being curious is not being essential.
hazards.far-end-axis: You stood in line with the tendon at the dead end. Both ends are on the axis. The live end is where the jack is and the end everybody remembers; the dead end is the one people walk past, and a strand that pulls through an anchorage exits there just as hard.
hazards.green-concrete: You started stressing on the calendar instead of on a strength result. Concrete that has not reached the strength the drawings require at transfer cannot carry the anchorage: the bearing plate punches through the slab face and takes the tendon and the concrete around it with it.
hazards.hand-seat: You went at a loaded anchorage with a hammer. The wedges are seated hydraulically by the jack, and struck by hand they can come out of the cavity at the person holding the hammer. Nothing is dressed, tapped or adjusted on an anchorage that is holding load.

interrupts.alert: A labourer has walked round the end of the barricade and is standing in line with the tendon behind your jack, looking at his phone.
interrupts.cue: Somebody is in the cone with the ram loaded.
interrupts.missNote: You kept pulling with a man standing in the line of the tendon. Nothing came out of the anchorage this time, which is the only reason this is a lesson rather than a fatality — and he had no idea he was standing anywhere in particular, because the barricade he walked round was the only thing that was ever going to tell him.
interrupts.why: A person in the cone while the tendon is loaded is the one condition on this deck that outranks everything, including the tendon. Pressure comes off first and the argument happens afterwards: the ram is holding tens of kips that leave along that line if anything in the anchorage lets go.
interrupts.wrongNote: It is the pump stop. Take the pressure off before you do anything else about the man in the cone.

interrupts.alert: Strand has appeared past the wedge mark on the tendon you just seated, and the tail has crept out of the anchor head.
interrupts.cue: The anchorage you just set is moving.
interrupts.missNote: The slipped tendon went unmarked and the tails were cut with the rest of them. That tendon can no longer be re-stressed or even measured, the slab is short of the force the drawings call for by an amount nobody can now establish, and the record says it was accepted.
interrupts.why: A wedge that draws after seating is a tendon giving its force back, and it is also a tendon that may keep moving. It gets tagged where the next crew will see it and left for the engineer to decide on — because the one thing that would make it unrecoverable is somebody cutting the tail off in the meantime.
interrupts.wrongNote: It is the hold tag. Mark the tendon so nobody cuts it, then get the engineer.

lateNotes.cut-tail: Tails come off after the elongations are measured, recorded and accepted. Cut early and the tendon can never be re-stressed.
lateNotes.jack: The jack goes on once the anchorages have been inspected and both end zones are barricaded.
lateNotes.pump-throttle: The pump comes up after the strength is proven, the zones are set, the jack is mounted and the crew is out of both cones.

name: Post Tension

passRule.note: stars >= 2 and no unsafe action (WebXR/shared/records.js passed())

steps.cue: Read the tendon, the strand, the jacking force, the calculated elongation and the strength required before stressing.
steps.prompt: Read the tendon, the strand, the jacking force, the calculated elongation and the strength required before stressing.
steps.title: Take the stressing record and the tendon schedule
steps.why: The stressing record is the drawing for this operation and the document the job is accepted on. Every number that decides whether the tendon is right — force, calculated elongation, the tolerance that elongation is judged against — is on it before anyone touches a pump.

steps.cue: Read the cylinder break and the maturity meter for this placement, and commit on the strength.

gauge.label: f'ci
gauge.missNote: That is under the 3,000 psi this record requires before transfer. Stressing it now pulls the anchorage out through the face of the slab — wait for the next break or the meter.

steps.prompt: Read the cylinder break and the maturity meter for this placement, and commit on the strength.
steps.title: Prove the concrete has reached stressing strength
steps.why: Concrete is stressed on a strength result, never on how many days it has been. ACI 318 requires the specified compressive strength at transfer before the tendons take load, and cylinders or a maturity meter are how that is known — a slab poured in cold weather can be days behind the calendar and look identical.

steps.cue: Serial numbers on the certificate against the ram and the gauge in front of you, and the date still in.
steps.prompt: Serial numbers on the certificate against the ram and the gauge in front of you, and the date still in.
steps.title: Check the jack and gauge calibration
steps.why: The gauge is the only thing telling you how hard you are pulling, and it only means anything as half of the pair it was calibrated with. A gauge off its ram, or a certificate out of date, turns the whole operation into a guess — and the elongation check downstream cannot tell you which of the two lied.

steps.cue: Walk the live ends and the dead ends and click anything that is not fit to take load.

itemNames.unsound-bearing: honeycombed concrete behind a bearing plate

itemNotes.damaged-sheath: The sheathing on the far tendon is split where it enters the anchorage and the strand under it is rusted. Corroded strand at the anchorage is where an unbonded tendon fails.
itemNotes.fouled-pocket: The second live-end pocket has slurry set in the wedge cavity. Wedges seated on grout do not bite on strand, and they let go later rather than now.
itemNotes.unsound-bearing: There is honeycombing in the concrete behind a dead-end bearing plate. That plate has nothing solid to bear on, and it is the dead end that everybody forgets to look at.

steps.prompt: Walk the live ends and the dead ends and click anything that is not fit to take load.
steps.title: Inspect both ends before anything is pressurised
steps.why: Every one of these is a five-minute job now and an anchorage failure later. The anchorage is the only part of a tendon anybody can see, so it is the only part that gets inspected — which is exactly why it has to be inspected properly.

steps.cue: Barricade the space behind the jack, then the space in line with the dead end, then sign the approaches.
steps.outOfOrderNote: Live end first, then the dead end, then the signs. The end you are about to stand a jack on is the end that gets protected before anything else.
steps.prompt: Barricade the space behind the jack, then the space in line with the dead end, then sign the approaches.
steps.title: Barricade both cones, live end first
steps.why: The exclusion zone for a stressing operation is a cone off each end of the tendon, because that is the direction the energy leaves in. Live end first: that is where the jack is going and where somebody is about to be working. The signs go up last because they are what keep everybody who is not on this crew out of both.

steps.cue: Paint a reference mark on the strand where it leaves the anchorage, before the jack goes on.
steps.prompt: Paint a reference mark on the strand where it leaves the anchorage, before the jack goes on.
steps.title: Mark the strand for the elongation measurement
steps.why: Elongation is a difference between two positions of the same mark, so the mark is made before any load is on the tendon. No mark, no measurement, and no way of knowing afterwards whether this tendon got the force the engineer designed for.

steps.cue: Carry the ram to the live end and seat it square on the bearing plate, with the strand through the nose.

drag.missNote: Not seated on the bearing plate — square it up on the anchorage before any pressure goes near it.

steps.prompt: Carry the ram to the live end and seat it square on the bearing plate, with the strand through the nose.
steps.title: Mount the jack on the tendon
steps.why: A jack that is not square on the plate loads the anchorage on one side and can jump off it under pressure. Seating it properly is also the last work anybody does at that end of the tendon — from here on the operation is run from beside it.

steps.cue: Move everybody out of both cones to the marked position beside the tendon, and say out loud that you are pulling.
steps.prompt: Move everybody out of both cones to the marked position beside the tendon, and say out loud that you are pulling.
steps.title: Put the crew at right angles and call the zone clear
steps.why: Beside the tendon is the only place to stand: ninety degrees to the axis, out of both cones, where you can see the ram and the gauge. The call is not a courtesy — it is how the person who wandered onto your deck finds out that the slab in front of them is about to be loaded.

steps.cue: Bring the pump up steadily and hold the force on the record while the ram runs out.
steps.holdBreakNote: The force has dropped off the record's figure. Bring it back up smoothly and hold it there while the ram runs out.
steps.prompt: Bring the pump up steadily and hold the force on the record while the ram runs out.
steps.title: Ramp the jack to the specified force
steps.why: The force comes up smoothly and stops at the figure on the record. Snatching at it overshoots a tendon there is no way of un-stressing, and stopping short leaves a slab that is not carrying what it was designed to carry — and both of those are read afterwards, off the elongation.

steps.cue: Read the scale against your mark from beside the jack, and commit the measured elongation.

gauge.label: ELONGATION
gauge.missNote: That is outside the 5.12 to 5.89 in this record accepts against a 5.50 in calculated elongation. Do not seat it and do not cut it — stop and call the engineer.

steps.prompt: Read the scale against your mark from beside the jack, and commit the measured elongation.
steps.title: Measure the elongation against the record
steps.why: This is the proof. The measured elongation is compared with the elongation calculated on the stressing record, and a reading outside the range that record accepts stops the operation: it means the tendon is binding somewhere in the slab, the jack and gauge are out, or the strand in the duct is not the strand on the drawing. Which of those it is, is the engineer's to work out. The seven per cent on this record is the discrepancy at which ACI 318 requires the cause to be found rather than argued about.

steps.cue: Hold the seating pressure until the wedges are drawn fully down into the anchor head.
steps.holdBreakNote: You came off the seating pressure early. Wedges that are not fully drawn will let the strand slip — take it back up and hold it.
steps.prompt: Hold the seating pressure until the wedges are drawn fully down into the anchor head.
steps.title: Seat the wedges at the design force
steps.why: The wedges are what hold the tendon for the next eighty years, and they are set hydraulically, at full force, in one movement. Wedges that are not fully home let the strand draw back through them, and the slab quietly loses the force the record says it has.

steps.cue: Wind the release valve open and let the ram come back under control, with nobody behind it.
steps.prompt: Wind the release valve open and let the ram come back under control, with nobody behind it.
steps.title: Release the pressure and retract the ram
steps.why: The anchorage takes the load at the moment the jack gives it up, and that is when a badly seated wedge announces itself. The pressure comes off slowly, from the side, with the cone still empty — the barricades come down after the jack does, not before.

steps.cue: Get the measured elongations on the record and accepted, then cut the tails, then fill the pockets.
steps.outOfOrderNote: Acceptance first. Once a tail is cut there is no re-stressing that tendon and no measurement left to argue with.
steps.prompt: Get the measured elongations on the record and accepted, then cut the tails, then fill the pockets.
steps.title: Record and accept, then cut and grout
steps.why: In that order, because cutting is irreversible: a tendon with its tail cut off can never be re-stressed or re-measured, so nothing is cut until the engineer has the numbers and has taken them. Grout goes in last and seals the anchorage against the water that would corrode it.

steps.cue: Walk both ends of every tendon you have stressed and click anything that has moved or broken out.

itemNotes.slipped-wedge: One anchorage has strand showing past the wedge mark — that wedge has drawn since it was set, and the tendon behind it is not holding what the record says.
itemNotes.spalled-pocket: The concrete at the corner of a pocket has spalled away from the plate. The bearing area is smaller than the design assumed, and it is working on what is left.

steps.prompt: Walk both ends of every tendon you have stressed and click anything that has moved or broken out.
steps.title: Walk the stressed tendons before the deck is handed over
steps.why: A tendon tells you it is unhappy in the first hour, at the anchorage, and it tells somebody standing there looking at it. After the pockets are closed nobody will see these ends again for the life of the building.

tagline: Stressing tendons in a cast-in-place slab: strength proven before transfer, calibrated jack and gauge, both end cones barricaded and nobody behind the ram, force ramped, elongation measured against the record, and nothing cut until the engineer accepts it
